questions.question: What problem is LangGraph primarily designed to solve?
options: Stateful multi-step workflows with control flow and persistence.
questions.explanation: LangGraph models workflows as graphs with explicit nodes, edges, and shared state so you can build multi-step agents that branch, loop, pause for human input, and resume from checkpoints.

questions.question: In LangGraph, what is the role of state?
options: Shared workflow data passed and updated across nodes.
questions.explanation: State is the typed data contract that flows through every node; each node reads what it needs and writes back updates, so the entire graph communicates through a single evolving snapshot.

questions.question: When do conditional edges add value?
options: When routing depends on risk, confidence, policy, or missing data.
questions.explanation: Conditional edges encode branching logic that depends on runtime state — for example routing to a human-review node when confidence is low — making each decision point explicit and independently testable.

questions.question: Why are thread IDs important in LangGraph persistence?
options: They identify checkpoint history used for resume and replay.
questions.explanation: A thread ID labels a specific execution history in the checkpointer; passing the same ID on the next run loads the saved state so the workflow resumes exactly where it paused.

questions.question: What does an interrupt enable in a workflow?
options: Pause execution and wait for external/human input before continuing.
Force model output to be deterministic.
questions.explanation: An interrupt halts the graph at a designated node and waits for an external signal or human approval before proceeding; without it, all automated decisions execute without any oversight.

questions.question: What is a common anti-pattern in LangGraph design?
options: Putting all logic into one node and using unclear state.
Adding conditional routes for policy checks.
questions.explanation: Cramming all logic into one giant node defeats the purpose of a graph — you lose the ability to test nodes independently, trace failures to a specific step, or reuse parts of the workflow.

questions.question: Why is streaming useful in LangGraph systems?
options: It provides real-time progress visibility and debugging signals.
It removes the need for checkpoints.
questions.explanation: Streaming emits state updates as each node completes, giving users visible progress on long-running workflows and giving developers a live trace to identify which node is slow or producing bad output.

questions.question: When should you choose LangGraph over a simple chain?
options: For every single-turn text rewrite task.
Only when no tools are used.
When workflow needs branching, resume, approvals, or long-running state.
questions.explanation: A simple chain is sufficient for linear, stateless tasks; LangGraph is justified when you need conditional routing, checkpoint-based resume, human-in-the-loop gates, or state that persists across multiple turns.
